Really great story game where you play as an investigator for a Dystopian government to stop terrorist attacks. You get to use an in depth surveillance system to not only look at what the characters post on "blogs," and websites, but also tap into their phone and even desktop later on. You get to choose what information to highlight and store on each POI which can lead to different endings. There is a bit of moral ambiguity in each decision you make especially once you see the outcome, and with reminders of what you did as you progress.

Overall pretty fast/easy to complete taking around 4hrs for me, and with the ability to replay specific levels once you finish one ending so it's easier to go back and explore other endings as well as getting any achievements you missed.

I would rate this game 9/10. It's almost perfect. The gameplay is new and different. The story is interesting and keeps you guessing. It doesn't take more than a few hours to play through the entire story. Replayability is high as well, as you definitely want to try making different choices to see if they yield a different outcome. The only drawbacks for me were 1) you can't skip to the end of calls/texts, which is a bit tedious on your third or fourth playthrough and 2) I still have some unanswered questions about the story.

This game is... Well, it's different.
I understand that some people have their objections against it but it's interesting. At first you start it as any "adventure" game and focus on simply picking up information (and think this game is silly because it all boils down to simply pulling highlited items from one window to another; ok, it's got a story but that's as much "interactive" as it gets).
Then you notice that you get to chose not only which of conflicting parts of data you pass on to the system, but also how many of them you decide to omit.
Then you notice that your choices do have an impact on the story and how it unfolds.
Of course, you may treat this as a manifesto against surveilance but can also treat it as an interesting experiment in balancing the needs of the many with the needs of ones. And a study about security and privacy. And your own approach. Because the more you get involved with the story, the more interesting it gets.
The only flaw I see is that you can't manually save and revert to a point in time to make different choice and see its result. I can understand why it was done this way but since you'd need to play the game from the very beginning, the game loses its replayability value.
I probably wouldn't buy this game for its full price but I'm glad I played it.

This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

Orwell is for players who like investigation and mystery. If you don't enjoy extensive reading, you're not going to have fun. However, if you love researching bits of evidence across numerous faux websites, phone conversations, text messages, emails, and more, this is the game for you. The opportunities to spy on everyone and everything quickly become unnervingly attractive.

One catch: Orwell has multiple endings and the story can go a number of different ways, but progression can feel frustratingly limited at times. While the player does have the freedom to decide which evidence to submit/ignore, they are often required to stick to a specific list in order to move forward. However, the upside to this is that progression is nearly always intuitive. 

While not perfect, Orwell allows players to become an omniscient government agent who can truly see all, using formidable tools to influence a nation. I highly recommend this game with a solid 8/10 rating.

I would give this game a 4.5/5. It was incredibly engaging and had a great emotional effect on me. I went into the game feeling icky about mass surveillance, but the devs smartly motivate you to want to use Orwell to solve a bombing the second the game opens. Now that you are hooked in, you will probably like me finish the whole game in one sitting and experience an emotional rollercoaster. 

MINOR SPOILERS:

My one main complaint about the game is that occasionally, you will get "stuck" and get frustrated (don't worry, you can't actually get stuck). I was trying really hard to only put relevant data in the Orwell database and sometimes I would have put everything in that I wanted to use, and the game would not progress. I would now be randomly putting info into the database to progress the story, resulting in me regretting some of my uploads. This could have been solved by giving the player more background information about the game and the game world so that it was more obvious what is relevant at times. There are also a few classic video game annoyances where you upload something and your boss completely twists that information into something it didn't mean, but at least in this game that is the point.

MAJOR SPOILERS:

By the mid to late game, I successfully felt "icky" about my actions, so the game is really good. The game is basically rigged so that on your first play through, you will probably provide too much information about a murderer and cause the cops to kill said person when they are arrested, which makes you reflect on your indirect involvement in their death. Again, providing more info at the start of the game would have probably helped people not accidentally kill this person, but I think this was the best part of the game in terms of how it sticks with you after you finish it. It definitely showed how your "well-meaning" efforts to catch the "bad guys" can become a slippery slope.

The problem I have with this game is that it tries to hold you accountable for choices you did not make. Your task in Orwell is simply to retrieve information, someone will make a decision based on the information you collect. However, you are not in control of when this person makes a decision, so at times your attempt to gather all information to get the full picture are halted midway.  In addition, you are forced to choose between information chunks at crucial moments in the game even though there is no reason why you should. By doing so, the game forces you to not consider the entire context. And what does the game do to you at end? Blame you for not considering the entire context.

Another problem I have with this game is the more philosophical debate of an Orwellian surveillance system. By pretending that there is no separation of power or strict legislation on how evidence may be gathered, the creators abuse the fictive setting to criticize such a system. Yes, such a system would be horrible in certain dictatorship countries that currently exist, but we already know that don't we? It's an interesting concept that can be used for good as well. This nuance is missing in the story and as a result the writers and this game discredit themselves as a worthy piece of fiction.

It was an enjoyable and unique game. It definitely makes you consider our current surveillance in the world and how it's all headed to exactly what George Orwell predicted in 1984. There is a lot of reading, so if that is not your thing, then this game is absolutely not for you. I wish it had more replayability and I wish it was longer.

The puzzles are fun, the gameplay is fun, and the UI is good. But every time I see this game in my library it almost feels like I wish I never got the game. There was a specific choice in the game that had some current day political bias in it, and although it definitely wasn't over-bearing, it did make me think less of the game.

Now as my memory of the story has faded all I am left remembering of this game was the excellent sound and UI design, and the one foolish story decision which I disagreed with. Despite this, I'd still rate the game 7/10. But in a market with more 9/10 and 10/10 games than you could ever play, why would you ever spend money playing a *good* game when you can buy a *great* game?

[h1]No one is anonymous[/h1]

Orwell is a game where our task is to find the culprits of a bomb attack. We start with a certain woman who was at the scene of the bombing and was captured on the cameras. We discover more clues related to this woman, and with them we get to more people who may be involved in the terrorist attack. 

The game is not complicated, especially because the system we use to find new clues highlights new information about specific people, and our task is only to match the information to the person. This does not mean that the game is linear. We can skip some important information, which has its effect in the future. Successive people and the information we discover about them make the game really engaging despite its simplicity. It is worth noting that the game is not long, but thanks to that it does not get boring too quickly.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

Orwell is a game that shows how easy it is to get information about someone. He points out that even someone who seems to be anonymous on the Internet always leaves some information that reveals his true face. Personally, he thinks that it is a good and well-thought-out game, but this style of gameplay will not appeal to everyone. The low price also encourages to play the game.
